sources.citation: Kouanga, Julien. 2017. Morphologie nominale du Yākpà de Kembe. Mémoire de Master 2, Université de Bangui (SIL Language & Culture Archives). 260 pp. [Glottolog ref 680644; Yakpa = Mid-Southern Banda [bjo]]
sources.note: Ch. 1 phonology: 1.3 'Les tons' pp. 36-39 -- Yakpa is a tone language with three level tones (haut, moyen, bas) and two contour tones (montant haut-bas, descendant bas-haut) plus a moyen-bas contour in French loans; 1.4 pp. 39-40 canonical forms CV, CVCV, CVCVCV, open syllables. Nothing on word stress/accent anywhere (whole-text grep for accent|tonique|intensit|proémin|prosod: only sec. 3.4.3.7 pp. 112-113, where French loanwords' 'accents' are mapped onto Yakpa tones).

sources.note: '2a. There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages -- High, Mid, and Low.... 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here. Compare Eboué's BANDA spellings yaUra (dog), yabru (goat), akblo (child) with Hackett's TOGBO renderings...' -- generic BANDA (Eboué's Banda; Hackett's Togbo = togb1241), no placement rule, not tied to a Mid-Southern variety.

sources.note: Most detailed Banda description; Linda is the closest sister language (Banda-Bambari [liy], Glottolog band1344, same Lindaic node). Its phonology chapter would give the prosodic statement for the nearest relative (Arom 2007, following it, says Banda-Linda 'does not use accents'). Not a description of Mid-Southern Banda itself.
